```{r Alternative 1 Comparison, fig.width = 9}
  theme_hospital_bio()

print(alt1_combined)
```

We placed our three dimensionality reduction methods side-by-side to establish a clear baseline comparison of how each algorithm handles the dataset's variance. Looking at the scatter plots, we can see that while PCA captures the massive linear shift caused by the treatments along the axes, it compresses the data too much to fully isolate the cell lines. In contrast, t-SNE and UMAP excel at unpacking these tighter, local sub-clusters, cleanly dividing the Jurkat and J-LatA2 cells within each distinct treatment island.


#### 9.2.2 Alternative 2

```{r Alternative 2 Comparison}
alt2_facet_plot <- ggplot(df_long, aes(x = Dim1, y = Dim2, colour = treatment, shape = cell_type)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.8, size = 2, stroke = 0.5) +
  stat_ellipse(geom = "polygon", alpha = 0.10, level = 0.95, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.35) +
  facet_wrap(~ Method, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = treatment_colours, name = "Treatment") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = cell_shapes, name = "Cell type") +
  labs(
    title = "Alternative 2: Tidy Facet-Wrap Comparison",
    subtitle = "95% confidence ellipses showing group separation",
    x = "Dimension 1", y = "Dimension 2"
  ) +
  theme_hospital_bio() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
        legend.position = "right")

print(alt2_facet_plot)
```

To better evaluate the statistical robustness of these groupings, we added 95% confidence intervals using a tidy facet-wrap approach. These shaded ellipses are incredibly helpful for us to visually prove our observations: in the PCA plot, the confidence regions stretch and slightly converge, whereas in the t-SNE and UMAP projections, the ellipses confirm that our treatment macro-clusters are highly cohesive, strictly separated, and have perfectly defined boundaries.


#### 9.2.3 Alternative 3

```{r Alternative 3 Comparison}
compute_centroids <- function(df) {
  df |> dplyr::group_by(treatment, cell_type) |>
    dplyr::summarise(centroid_x = mean(Dim1, na.rm = TRUE),
                     centroid_y = mean(Dim2, na.rm = TRUE),
                     .groups = "drop") |>
    dplyr::mutate(group = paste(treatment, cell_type, sep = "_"))
}

build_spider_plot <- function(df, method_label) {
  centroids_df <- compute_centroids(df)
  spider_df <- df |> dplyr::left_join(centroids_df, by = c("treatment", "cell_type"))
  
  ggplot() +
    geom_segment(data = spider_df,
                 aes(x = Dim1, y = Dim2, xend = centroid_x, yend = centroid_y, colour = treatment),
                 alpha = 0.3, linewidth = 0.3) +
    geom_point(data = spider_df, aes(x = Dim1, y = Dim2, colour = treatment, shape = cell_type),
               size = 1.5, alpha = 0.7) +
    geom_point(data = centroids_df, aes(x = centroid_x, y = centroid_y, colour = treatment),
               shape = 8, size = 4, stroke = 1.2) +
    ggrepel::geom_label_repel(data = centroids_df,
                              aes(x = centroid_x, y = centroid_y, label = group, colour = treatment),
                              size = 2.8, fontface = "bold", fill = "white", alpha = 0.8, show.legend = FALSE) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = treatment_colours, name = "Treatment") +
    scale_shape_manual(values = cell_shapes, name = "Cell type") +
    labs(title = method_label, x = "Dim 1", y = "Dim 2") +
    theme_hospital_bio() +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12))
}

alt3_pca   <- build_spider_plot(df_pca, "PCA") + theme(legend.position = "none")
alt3_tsne  <- build_spider_plot(df_tsne, "t-SNE") + theme(legend.position = "none")
alt3_umap  <- build_spider_plot(df_umap, "UMAP") + theme(legend.position = "right")

alt3_combined <- (alt3_pca | alt3_tsne | alt3_umap) + 
  plot_annotation(title = "Alternative 3: Centroid Spider Plots",
                  subtitle = "Colors = Treatment, Shapes = Cell type")
print(alt3_combined)
```

We designed these centroid spider networks to explicitly map the internal geometry and spatial spread of each distinct biological subgroup. By anchoring every single cell to its calculated group centroid, we can immediately spot the intra-cluster variance. In the non-linear projections, the exceptionally short "spider legs" visually confirm the high density of the clusters and show us exactly where the Jurkat and J-LatA2 populations spatially diverge within the broader drug conditions.

::: {style="background-color: #eaf2f8; color: #21618c; padding: 15px; border-left: 4px solid #3498db; border-radius: 4px; margin-bottom: 15px;"}
Finally, we generated an interactive version of the faceted plots so we could actively explore the detailed metadata of any individual data point directly on the graph. While the overall structure mirrors our previous plots, this format is an essential tool for us when checking for potential batch outliers; it allows us to simply hover over any stray coordinate to instantly verify its exact replicate and experimental condition without cluttering the visual space.
:::

### 9.3 Comparison analysis
::: well
#### 9.3.1 Conclusions about the data itself:

* **Treatment is the absolute driver:** The three plots consistently show that the latency-reversing drugs (PMA and SAHA) are the massive drivers of transcriptomic change, far outweighing baseline cell differences. 

* **PMA triggers a massive transcriptional shock:** PMA-treated samples form the most isolated and distant clusters across all three methods. SAHA also cleanly separates from the DMSO controls, though with a milder effect compared to PMA's extreme reactivation.

* **Cell type identity is secondary:** Because Jurkat and J-LatA2 share a nearly identical baseline, their intrinsic differences only become structurally apparent *after* isolating the treatment groups. 

* **Biological signal beats batch effects:** Inside each treatment group, replicates form small sub-groups, confirming a manageable technical batch effect. However, a PMA sample from replicate 1 is fundamentally clustered with other PMA samples, proving biology > technical noise.
:::


::: well
#### 9.3.2 How the techniques show our specific data:

* **PCA:** Provides the linear big picture. It captures the massive treatment variance along PC1, cleanly splitting the heavily reactivated PMA samples from SAHA and DMSO. However, because it compresses local variance to prioritize global structure, the secondary cell-type differences remain harder to resolve globally.

* **t-SNE:** Unpacks the compressed PCA clouds by focusing on local neighborhoods. It explicitly forms distinct macro-clusters for each treatment and, crucially, resolves clear sub-clusters for Jurkat and J-LatA2 *within* those treatment islands.

* **UMAP:** Offers the best overall topological balance. It preserves the strong global treatment hierarchy (like PCA) while maintaining the tight, highly resolved local cell-type sub-clusters (like t-SNE) within each drug condition.
:::

::: well
#### 9.3.3 Do we get to the same conclusions with the three methods?

**Yes, absolutely.** Although PCA, t-SNE, and UMAP use different mathematical approaches and produce different geometric distributions, all three lead to identical biological conclusions:

* **The primary biological driver is identical:** All algorithms agree that the experimental treatment—not the basal viral integration—forces the most extreme displacement in the transcriptome.

* **The treatment hierarchy remains constant:** All three methods consistently show PMA causing the most extreme shift, SAHA driving a distinct intermediate state, and DMSO remaining at baseline.

* **The batch effect behaves the same way:** In all three maps, replicates do not mix perfectly, proving that batch effects are a real but strictly secondary technical variation that must be computationally corrected prior to differential expression analysis.
:::
